# Why Bestla is spelled that way — and what it costs to get it right

There is a version of this name the early internet had to settle for: *bestla*. This is the file on how **Bestla** replaced it.

Bestla has no myth of her own — no journey, no contest, no speech survives in her name. What the sources give instead is a position so consequential that the entire pantheon hangs from it: she is the point where the family tree of the gods roots itself in the giants' world.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Bestla
- **ASCII form:** bestla
- **Meaning:** "Bark, bast"
- **Domain of influence:** Mother of Odin, Giantess
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** ᛒᛁᛋᛏᛚᛅ
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 66 of 406

## The Name Before the Marks


Spoken, the name runs `/ˈbest.lɑ/` — 'BEST-la' — two short syllables, stress on the first; the 'e' of 'best', then a light open 'ah'.

## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Bestla** lives at [/bestla/](/bestla/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/bestla/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/bestla/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/bestla/patterns/).

One decisive feature survives — a single, honest mark — which places the restoration in Tier-2: exact, and exactly labeled.

## Where the Name Stood First

Bestla is an entirely textual figure: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, no place-name is securely hers, and no image can be identified with her. Her attestations are the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), which alone preserves Hávamál 140, and the manuscripts of Snorri's Edda — the Codex Regius (GKS 2367 4to, early 14th c.), Codex Wormianus, Codex Trajectinus, and the Uppsala Edda — which carry Gylfaginning's genealogy and the þulur that list her among the giantesses. The indirect material context is the same as for the whole jötunn complex: the myth of divine descent from giant-kind belongs to the world of poetry and learned prose, not to dedicatory practice, and no inscription yet found names Bǫlþorn or his daughter. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

## The Archetype at Work

The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) seats this temple in **3 industries**, each match argued and weighted: **Ancestry & Heritage Services** (the giant grandmother of the gods — the seam that makes the Æsir half-giant.); **Environmental & Climate Services** (a troll-woman of the frost line — the ice of Ginnungagap in the gods' own blood.); **History, Archives & Records** (one sentence in Gylfaginning 6 — the entire dossier, and genealogy's most consequential single line.). The [Resonance File](/bestla/blog/resonance/) reads those seats through the myths themselves.

## In the Sacred Texts

The Norse tradition is not a vibe; it is a library. The [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/) holds [Poetic Edda](/texts/poetic-edda/) and [Prose Edda](/texts/prose-edda/) — the primary sources the temple's scholarship is built on. The temple is the argument; the texts are the evidence.
